content.title: About
content.content: Beans and brown rice are a combination of legumes and a whole grain, rich in plant protein, fiber, and complex carbohydrates. Various beans (such as red, black, or white) provide a wide range of vitamins and minerals, while brown rice retains its bran and germ, making it more nutritious than white rice.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beans belong to the legume family and are among the oldest cultivated crops.
Brown rice is whole grain rice with the bran and germ intact, giving it higher levels of B‑vitamins and magnesium.
Together, beans and rice form a complete set of essential amino acids, creating a complete protein source for vegetarians.
Beans may help lower cholesterol thanks to their soluble fiber content.
When stored properly, brown rice stays fresh for up to 6 months, and dry beans can be kept for a year.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Beans provide about 20 g of protein per 100 g, and brown rice adds another 2‑3 g, supporting muscle repair and satiety.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Both foods contain soluble and insoluble fiber that promotes healthy digestion and stabilizes blood sugar.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Beans are high in iron, folate, and magnesium, while brown rice supplies magnesium, selenium, and B‑vitamins.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Fiber and phytochemicals in beans help reduce LDL‑cholesterol levels.

items.title: Blood‑glucose regulation
items.content: The complex carbs of brown rice and the slowly digested proteins of beans lead to a gradual rise in blood sugar after meals.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Both beans and whole grains contain phytates, which can inhibit mineral absorption; soaking and sprouting reduce this effect.

items.title: Anti‑nutrients and gas
items.content: Certain beans contain oligosaccharides that may cause gas; proper soaking and thorough cooking mitigate this.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Arsenic content in rice
items.content: Brown rice can contain higher levels of organic arsenic; rinsing well and rotating with other grains is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beans and brown rice are commonly cooked together as a pilaf, soup, or salad. Soak beans for at least 6‑8 hours, then boil until tender. Rinse brown rice and cook in a 1:2 rice‑to‑water ratio for about 40‑45 minutes. Add herbs, vegetables, and lean protein for a balanced meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 12 months. Keep brown rice in a sealed package in a cool, dark pantry or refrigerator, where it stays fresh for up to 6 months. Discard any beans or rice that develop off‑odors, mold, or rancidity.

chicken-tenders-or-strips-breaded-from-f.title: Chicken tenders or strips, breaded, from fast food

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken tenders (or strips) are pieces of chicken breast coated in a seasoned breading made from flour, spices and sometimes breadcrumbs, then deep‑fried until golden and crispy. They are sold at most fast‑food chains and are often served with dipping sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial chicken tender recipe appeared in the United States in the 1970s.
Some restaurants use corn starch in the coating for an extra crunchy crust.
Popular dipping sauces include barbecue, honey‑mustard, sweet‑and‑sour, and ranch.
In Japan a thinner version called “tenderloin” is common, featuring longer, slimmer strips.
Chicken tenders are a staple of kids’ menus because of their soft texture and bite‑size shape.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Chicken meat provides high‑quality complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken is rich in niacin (B3) and pyridoxine (B6), which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: When not coated with sugary batters, tenders fit well into low‑carb eating patterns.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Chicken supplies phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bone health and immunity.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat in the breading helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: Deep‑frying adds significant saturated fat and calories, which can contribute to weight gain if eaten frequently.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Salt used in the breading and sauces can lead to excessive sodium intake.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: If partially hydrogenated oils are used for frying, trans fats may form, which are harmful to heart health.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people may be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tenders are typically served hot, dipped in sauces, added to salads, or used as a filling in wraps. Their finger‑food format makes them a popular snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked tenders in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. They can be frozen for up to 2 months and reheated in an oven or microwave.

content.title: About
content.content: Almond cookie is a crisp biscuit that incorporates ground almonds or almond pieces into the dough. It has a gentle sweet flavor with a distinctive nutty aroma and is often finished with powdered sugar or a thin glaze.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Almond cookies appeared in Europe in the 19th century as a variation of traditional nut biscuits.
The almond not only adds flavor but also boosts the nutritional value of the cookie.
Traditionally the cookies are baked as small round or shaped pieces.
Some recipes use almond extract to intensify the almond taste.
Almond cookies are commonly served with tea or coffee as a light snack.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Almonds are a good source of vitamin E, an antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Provides healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: Monounsaturated fats in almonds may support heart health when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium in almonds is important for normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Provides protein and fiber
items.content: Almond cookie supplies plant protein and dietary fiber, helping to promote satiety.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Almonds contain more calcium than most nuts, which is beneficial for bone health.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: People with nut allergies may experience severe reactions to almond cookie.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: The cookie contains sugar and fat, so portion sizes should be moderated.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: High sugar levels may be unsuitable for individuals with diabetes or those following low‑sugar diets.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Almonds contain oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Almond cookie is convenient as a standalone snack, served with tea, coffee, or dessert sauces. It can be lightly warmed in the oven to restore crispness or used as a base for dessert tarts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cookies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life keep them in the refrigerator to prevent fat rancidity. Discard any cookies that show signs of mold or off‑odors.

content.title: About
content.content: Snapper is a marine fish from the Lutjanidae family, found in tropical and subtropical waters of the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans. It has firm, white flesh with a mild flavor, moderate fat content, and a characteristic pinkish skin.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Snapper can change sex during its life: younger individuals are often male, becoming female as they age.
In some regions the fish is called “royal” because of its popularity in fine dining.
There are more than 30 snapper species, the most well‑known being the Red Snapper (Lutjanus campechanus).
Snapper populations can rebound quickly when fisheries are properly managed.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Omega‑3s support heart health, reduce inflammation, and promote brain function.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Protein is essential for tissue growth, repair, and immune function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Snapper provides B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals: selenium and phosphorus
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant, while phosphorus is vital for bones and teeth.

items.title: Low mercury levels
items.content: Compared with larger predatory fish, snapper has lower mercury, making it a safer choice.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seafood, including snapper.

items.title: Possible parasites
items.content: Raw or undercooked snapper can harbor parasites; cook to an internal temperature of 63 °C.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Fresh fillet has moderate sodium; added sauces or marinades can increase intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Snapper is versatile: bake, grill, pan‑sear, or stew. Marinate fillets in lemon juice, olive oil, and herbs, then cook over medium heat for 8‑10 minutes. It is also used in sushi, ceviche, and fish soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh snapper in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C in a sealed container for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Before cooking, check for a fresh sea scent; any ammonia‑like odor indicates spoilage.

macaroni-or-pasta-salad-made-with-any-ty.title: Macaroni or Pasta Salad with Fat-Free Dressing

content.title: About
content.content: Macaroni or pasta salad with a fat‑free dressing is a light dish made from cooked pasta, fresh vegetables, and a dressing based on yogurt, kefir or balsamic vinegar without added oil. This combination keeps the meal low in calories while preserving a rich taste and satisfying texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pasta is one of the most widely consumed foods worldwide and can be made from wheat, rice, corn or legumes.
Fat‑free dressings often rely on dairy bases, adding probiotics and boosting nutritional value.
Pasta salads keep well in the refrigerator for 3‑4 days, making them ideal for work lunches.
Combining pasta with vegetables increases fiber and vitamin content.
A fat‑free version is suitable for calorie‑restricted diets and for people monitoring cholesterol levels.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: The absence of oil in the dressing dramatically reduces the dish’s calorie count, helping with weight management.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Pasta provides slowly digestible carbs that supply steady energy and help maintain stable blood sugar.

items.title: Fiber source
items.content: Added vegetables such as tomatoes, cucumbers, and peppers boost dietary fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Probiotics and calcium
items.content: A fat‑free dairy dressing contains live cultures and calcium, beneficial for bone health and gut microbiota.

items.title: Low sodium potential
items.content: When prepared at home you can control the amount of salt, making the dish heart‑friendly.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional wheat pasta contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Added sugars in dressings
items.content: Some commercial fat‑free dressings may contain added sugars; always check the label.

items.title: Acidity tolerance
items.content: Large amounts of acidic yogurt dressing may cause discomfort for those with high stomach acidity.

items.title: Portion control
items.content: Even though the dish is low‑calorie, overeating can still lead to excess calorie intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled or at room temperature. It can be eaten on its own, packed in a lunchbox, used as a side for fish or chicken, or mixed with leafy greens for a lighter meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Stir before serving to redistribute the dressing. Discard if the smell changes or mold appears.

content.title: About
content.content: Refried beans with meat is a classic Mexican dish consisting of cooked beans that are mashed and fried until creamy, then mixed with finely chopped meat (usually beef or pork). The dish has a rich, slightly smoky flavor and is used as a side, a main course, or a filling for tacos, burritos, and other dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The term “refried” comes from the Spanish “refritos,” meaning “fried again.”
Traditionally the beans are dried black or pinto beans that are soaked and boiled until soft before frying.
Original recipes use beef, but regional variations include pork, chicken, or even turkey.
It is often served with lime, cheese, sour cream, and fresh cilantro.
Refried beans became popular in the United States in the 1920s with the rise of Mexican restaurants.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Beans provide about 8 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are important for blood formation and nerve function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Beans raise blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for people prone to diabetes.

items.title: Meat adds B‑vitamins
items.content: B6 and B12 support energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared versions often contain added salt; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: If fatty meat is used, the dish can be high in saturated fats.

items.title: Anti‑nutrients
items.content: Raw beans contain phytates that reduce mineral absorption; proper soaking and cooking minimize them.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot as a side dish, taco or burrito filling, or as a main course with rice. Top with lime, fresh cilantro, shredded cheese, and sour cream for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked beans in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 3 months. Reheat thoroughly before eating to prevent bacterial growth.
